newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.N. aide optimistic on Iraq oil-for-food deal.
newsitem.headline: U.N. aide optimistic on Iraq oil-for-food deal.

text.p: United Nations Under-Secretary General Yasushi Akashi on Monday voiced optimism that the delayed "oil-for-food" deal meant to bring relief for the sufferings of ordinary Iraqis would go into force soon.

Akashi, top aide for humanitarian affairs to U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, told a news conference he hoped the agreement could be implemented "in the near future", adding later that it might be "a matter of weeks."

"We hope that in the near future....we shall be able to do it," said Akashi, one of three Japanese high in the hierarchy of the world body, who is in Geneva for a conference on coordination of relief in disaster situations.

Asked later for a more precise prediction, he replied: "I cannot speculate but I think it will be a matter of weeks." Boutros-Ghali, who played a key role in negotiating the deal, "is anxious to start this programme," he said.

Under the plan signed last May, U.N. economic sanctions imposed after Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990 and then was forced out in the Gulf War of early 1991 would be lifted to allow Baghdad to sell $2 billion of oil over six months.

Of this $1.13 billion would be earmarked under strict international supervision for the purchase of food and medical aid for an Iraqi population the U.N. itself recognises is largely living below the poverty line.

The rest would go to a U.N. fund administering reparations to individuals, firms and to Kuwait itself for damage suffered as a result of Iraq's seizure and six-month occupation of its southern neighbour state.

Implementation of the plan, which includes delivery of relief worth $260 million to Kurdish areas in the North, was suspended early this month after President Saddam Hussein sent troops to help one Kurdish faction seize power there.
The move brought retaliation in the form of United States air strikes against Iraqi military installations.

"The majority of people in Iraq are living below the poverty line, and recent military action has made the situation worse," said Akashi -- whose Department of Humanitarian Affairs (DHA) is seeking $39.9 million for emergency aid.
The DHA appeal to the international community, launched last week, is meant to help cover the coming three months while the "oil-for-food" deal is put in place.

"The cumulative effects of economic sanctions: hyper-inflation, unemployment and a 30 percent drop in crop production this year have led to a disquieting level of hardship now suffered by vulnerable groups in Iraq," the appeal said.

Akashi, former U.N. special envoy in Cambodia and Bosnia, told Monday's news conference the world body was "carefully assessing" whether all conditions were right for the long-negotiated May deal to be implemented.

A U.N. assessment team is currently in Iraq and was due to return to Baghdad on Monday following a visit to the north led by the world body's coordinator for Iraqi issues Gualtiero Fulcheri. He is due to send Boutros-Ghali a report on Tuesday.
